extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and members of the American Mathematical Society (AMS)
extracted.subtask_short: award selection criteria for math prizes
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptions and selection rationales for AMS prizes (Frank and Brennie Morgan Prize; Oswald Veblen Prize), showing the evaluative standards used to judge mathematical research (especially undergraduate research) including originality, impact, publication record, technical depth, and sustained contributions. Also includes procedural notes about committee-based selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of outstanding undergraduate mathematical research
rubrics_metrics.description: The Frank and Brennie Morgan Prize is intended to 'recognize and encourage outstanding mathematical research by undergraduate students.' Undergraduate research should meet high professional standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit examples of acceptable outputs include proving theorems, writing up results for publication, and giving talks on the work. The announcement emphasizes that undergraduate work can meet 'the highest standards of professional excellence.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of originality and solving long-standing problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Work is valued when it is original and addresses important, previously unresolved problems (e.g., solving a long-standing and much studied conjecture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citation example: Kannan Soundararajan (with R. Balasubramanian) 'solved a long-standing and much studied conjecture of Ron Graham.' Solving such problems is presented as strong evidence of exceptional research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication record in refereed/outstanding research journals
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong record of papers published, accepted, or submitted to top research journals is an important indicator of research quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: committee notes that an awardee 'has already had four papers appear in outstanding research journals, has had two other papers accepted, and has submitted three others.' Publication counts and venue quality are used as evidence of achievement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical sophistication, depth, and versatility
rubrics_metrics.description: Research should demonstrate high technical sophistication, depth of understanding, and intellectual versatility beyond typical expectations for the author's level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kiran Kedlaya's work is described as a 'portfolio of four professional level research papers that demonstrate sophistication, depth, and versatility far beyond what might be expected of a student.' The committee values these specific qualities in judging excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on the field and expert acclaim
rubrics_metrics.description: Work that brings acclaim from established researchers, changes how experts view a subject, or is said to 'rewrite' parts of the field is highly prized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrases used: 'has brought acclaim from experts,' 'his results have completely rewritten the subject.' Expert endorsement and demonstrable influence on the field are explicit evaluative signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making progress beyond professional peers
rubrics_metrics.description: Research that achieves results comparable to or exceeding what many professionals have done is a distinguishing criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citation: an undergraduate 'has made more progress than many professionals who have tackled it.' The committee notes relative performance against the professional community as a sign of exceptional merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustained and continuing contributions in a research area
rubrics_metrics.description: Prize-worthy work may consist of a sustained program of study and continuing contributions (not just a single result), showing ongoing advances in a research area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richard Hamilton is cited for his 'continuing study of the Ricci flow' and for ongoing analysis of singularities; long-term, cumulative impact is highlighted in the Veblen Prize citation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major theoretical advances: analysis, classification, existence/obstruction results, and foundational theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributions that provide deep analysis (e.g., of singularities), classification results, existence theorems, identification of obstructions, or foundational proofs in new subfields are criteria for major prizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the Veblen citation: Hamilton's classification of singularities for Ricci flow and Tian's settling of existence questions for Kähler–Einstein metrics on complex surfaces and finding obstructions; Tian (with Ruan) proving associativity in quantum cohomology are cited as types of achievements meriting the award.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection-building and conceptual advances across subfields
rubrics_metrics.description: Work that ties disparate areas together (e.g., linking existence theorems to geometric invariant theory or developing tools used across geometry/analysis) is recognized as highly valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tian's work linking Kähler–Einstein metrics to stability in geometric invariant theory and other cross-disciplinary advances are cited as important evaluative attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural selection: committee recommendation and council approval
rubrics_metrics.description: Award decisions are made via a formal procedure: a selection committee evaluates candidates and the AMS Council awards the prize based on the committee's recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Veblen Prize was 'awarded by the AMS Council on the basis of a recommendation by a selection committee,' and the Morgan Prize description lists the prize selection committee members. Committee composition and formal recommendation procedures are part of the evaluative process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signaling of research pathways and supporting evidence (mentorship, REU/internship experience, faculty recommendations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Participation in research programs (REUs, internships), mentoring relationships, and faculty recommendations are cited as relevant signals used to identify and contextualize candidates' research accomplishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Kiran Kedlaya's research was 'carried out in connection with summer research or internship programs for undergraduates' and he was 'recommended... by Joe Gallian,' indicating that such contexts and endorsements are considered by committees.
